title: Three hundred (Judges 7)
hook: God shrinks Gideon's army so no one will boast

segments.voice: Yesterday, Gideon in the winepress, and your line was you, mighty? Did you take a kind word without arguing? Day seven hundred five.

Gideon finally has an army, and God's complaint is not that it's too small. In the King James Bible: "The people that are with thee are too many for me to give the Midianites into their hands, lest Israel vaunt themselves against me, saying, Mine own hand hath saved me." Too many. Gideon's men are camped by a spring, and below them in the valley lies the camp of Midian and its allies, "like grasshoppers for multitude," the text says, with camels past counting. Any sensible general would be sending messengers for more troops. Gideon is told to send people home. Today's title is the number he's left with.

First cut: whoever is fearful and afraid may go home. The text says twenty-two thousand leave and ten thousand stay. Still too many, God says. Second cut: take them down to the water to drink. Some get down on their knees to drink. Some lap, the text says, putting their hand to their mouth. Three hundred lap. Those are the ones God keeps: "By the three hundred men that lapped will I save you." The text never explains why the lappers were chosen. Some preachers say they were the alert ones, keeping their eyes up. Others say the test was arbitrary on purpose, and God simply took the smaller group. Judges gives no reason at all. It isn't a test of who's best. The reason it does give is back in verse two: so that Israel can't say, mine own hand hath saved me. Then comes the plan, and it's strange. Each of the three hundred gets a trumpet and an empty pitcher with a lamp hidden inside. In the middle of the night they spread out around the camp, blow the trumpets, smash the pitchers so the lights blaze out, and cry: "The sword of the LORD, and of Gideon." And then: "they stood every man in his place round about the camp." They don't charge. They hold up their lights and stand still. The camp panics and turns on itself. Notice the order of that cry: the sword of the LORD first, Gideon second. The whole chapter is built so that, afterward, nobody can tell it as a story about their own strength. Less isn't a punishment here. Less is how they find out who did the saving.
screen: `THE TEXT NEVER SAYS WHY THE LAPPERS.`
then, large: `THE SWORD OF THE LORD, AND OF GIDEON.`
`THEY STOOD EVERY MAN IN HIS PLACE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: do something with less than you'd like. Settle, and breathe. Is there one thing on your plate today you feel under-equipped for: not enough time, not enough money, not enough help, not enough sleep? Name it. Then, instead of listing everything you lack, count what you actually have, the way Gideon counted at the water. Three hundred is a real number. So is one free hour, or two friends, or forty dollars. Ask what you could do with exactly that. If you pray, you can bring the gap to God. If you don't, simply breathe, and let the small number be enough for now. The bell holds the time.
Three hundred. The men who lapped the water: the army God made smaller, so no one could say, my own hand saved me.
Your line: less is enough. Today, start the thing you named with what you have, and don't wait for more. Day seven hundred five.

howItsDone: Some Christians tell the story of Gideon's three hundred to speak about God's strength showing up in human weakness, and some pair it with Paul's words in Second Corinthians that strength is made perfect in weakness.

original.note: Hebrew: my own hand saved me, the boast God shrinks the army to prevent (Judges 7:2).

trapdoor: what you thought: God chose the three hundred best soldiers.
what it means: God shrank the army so that no one could boast. the text never says the lappers were better.
what a scholar hears: Judges 7:2 gives the reason, lest Israel say, mine own hand hath saved me. the lapping test itself is never explained.

notes: Numbers (twenty-two thousand leave, ten thousand stay, three hundred lap) are taken directly from Judges 7:3, 7:6 and 7:7.
Judges 7:6 says those who lapped put 'their hand to their mouth', while 7:5 compares lapping to a dog; the script follows 7:6. Confirm.

The two popular explanations of the lapping test (the lappers were alert; God took the smaller group) are attributed to 'some preachers' and 'others', and the script says the text gives no reason. Confirm.
